images.title: Fifteen written three ways
images.purpose: Shows that one number, 15, can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers in more than one way.
images.composition: Plain white background, lots of empty space around the main object, no scenery, no characters, no extra text. One large number on the left joined by three arrows to three rows of number tiles on the right.
images.exact_structure: On the left, one large reddish purple (#CC79A7) circle holding 15. Three thin dark arrows go from the circle to three rows on the right, stacked one above the other with wide gaps. Row 1: two equal square teal (#0072B2) tiles holding 7 and 8 with a plus sign between them. Row 2: three equal square amber (#E69F00) tiles holding 4, 5 and 6 with plus signs between them. Row 3: five equal square green (#009E73) tiles holding 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 with plus signs between them. All tiles are the same size and all rows start at the same left edge, so row 3 is the longest. Nothing else in the frame.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: 15 can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers in three different ways.
images.description: Shows that one number, 15, can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers in more than one way.

image_decisions.why: Rows of consecutive number tiles that all make 15 show at a glance that one number can be split in several ways.
